one_paragraph_summary: Panganiban explains what a revolutionary government is and why Duterte might consider one. Ordinarily, a RevGov is installed by armed rebels who scrap the constitution and rule by might -- as the NPA's Sison threatens from the Netherlands. Alternatively, outsiders (civilians supported by the people and military) can wrest power without arms -- as Cory Aquino did in 1986: she won the snap election but was never proclaimed under the 1973 Constitution, taking power only after Marcos fled and the military pledged allegiance to her. A third type is the insider self-coup: the sitting president, backed by the military, sets aside the constitution, abolishes official terms, and rules by will. Duterte signaled this but backpedaled after the military declined. If it had succeeded, it would have meant abrogation of the 1987 Constitution, loss of all official terms (including his own), and exposure to coup attempts -- as Cory faced several after her own RevGov. Why risk it? To crush destabilizers and speed reforms: businessman Enrique Razon articulated the business case at the ASEAN 50 Summit -- 'The best infrastructures are in the countries ruled by dictatorships.' But a RevGov is a dictatorship and the 1987 Constitution's deliberate 'castration' of presidential powers means Duterte currently has far less clout than Marcos had in 1972 -- Marawi martial law gave him only about a quarter of that. If the RevGov fails, the risk shifts to the President; if it succeeds, the risk shifts to defenders of the Constitution. Cha-cha is also a radical alternative -- it could also abolish the presidency, Congress, and the Senate, remove all protected terms, and alter the Bill of Rights.
